taxonomy.subsystem: Gestational trophoblastic disease and genomic imprinting
taxonomy.subtopic: Androgenetic diploidy after fertilization of an empty ovum

questions.stem_html: A 24-year-old woman at 11 weeks of gestation has vaginal bleeding, severe vomiting and a uterus larger than expected. Beta-human chorionic gonadotropin is markedly elevated, and ultrasonography shows diffuse cystic intrauterine tissue without fetal parts. Karyotyping of villous tissue shows 46,XX. The accompanying parental-origin diagram depicts several fertilization mechanisms. Which mechanism most likely produced this conceptus?

options.text_html: Fertilization of an ovum lacking maternal nuclear DNA by one X-bearing sperm followed by paternal genome duplication
Fertilization of a normal ovum by two sperm, producing a diandric triploid conceptus
Meiotic nondisjunction in the maternal ovum followed by fertilization with a normal sperm
Mitotic loss of a paternal chromosome after normal biparental fertilization
Fertilization of a normal ovum followed by selective deletion of placental paternal alleles

questions.explanation_html: A complete hydatidiform mole is usually an androgenetic diploid conceptus. The most common mechanism is fertilization of an empty ovum by one X-bearing sperm followed by duplication of the paternal haploid genome, yielding 46,XX nuclear DNA entirely of paternal origin. Complete moles lack fetal parts, have diffuse hydropic villi and trophoblastic proliferation, produce very high hCG and lack p57 expression because p57 is maternally expressed.

wrong_choice_explanations.2: Dispermic fertilization of a normal ovum usually creates a partial mole with a triploid karyotype such as 69,XXY and may show fetal tissue.
wrong_choice_explanations.3: Maternal meiotic nondisjunction produces aneuploidy with retained maternal genetic contribution, not an androgenetic complete mole.
wrong_choice_explanations.4: Loss of one paternal chromosome would not create a diploid genome composed entirely of paternal chromosomes.
wrong_choice_explanations.5: Normal biparental fertilization retains maternal nuclear DNA and p57 expression.

questions.educational_objective: Complete hydatidiform moles are usually androgenetic diploid conceptions formed when an empty ovum is fertilized and the paternal genome duplicates; absence of maternal nuclear DNA explains absent p57 expression.
